498.title: Ashtpadi 16, salok: no form, no color
498.hook: roop na rekh na rang kichh: He has no form, no outline, no color (Sukhmani 16)
498.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the sixteenth ashtpadi with the salok roop na rekh na rang kichh, and gurdwaras keep no images of God, since no single form could contain the Formless.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taan: strength borrowed from the Giver is still strength. Today a new ashtpadi, the sixteenth, and a salok that seems to argue with this week.

Which is it? Two days ago, the picture was dye: everything soaked in His color. Today the very next ashtpadi opens by saying He has no color at all. Is God the dye that soaks every thread, or something with no color whatsoever? It can look like a contradiction. It's a pattern worth learning to spot, because Gurbani holds the two together on purpose.
screen: `TWO DAYS AGO: IN HIS COLOR.` → `TODAY: NO COLOR AT ALL.` → `WHICH IS IT?`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: He has no form, no outline, no color at all; God is beyond the three qualities. Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Three nos to start. Roop: form, shape, appearance. Rekh: a line, an outline, the edge you'd trace if you drew something. Rang: color. If you've been on this path since the start of the year, these may sound familiar. Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh's morning hymn, opened the same way: no mark, no sign, no color, no caste. Its short chachari lines said aroop hain, You are formless, and its opening verse even uses the salok's three words, roop, rang and rekh. So Guru Arjan and Guru Gobind Singh describe the One in the same breath of negatives. Now the puzzle: how can God have no color and also be the color everything happens in? Take light. White light has no color of its own; you can't point to it in a rainbow. And yet every color you see is that light, split and shining. Or water: no shape of its own, and it takes the shape of every glass. Having no color of your own is exactly what lets you be in every color. Something with a fixed outline can only be in one place; something with no outline can be everywhere. Gurdwaras keep no images of God. In this picture, that isn't because God is far from shapes. It's that no single shape could hold the One. Over the next two days, the salok's other phrases: beyond the three qualities, and known by those He blesses.
screen: `ROOP, REKH, RANG: FORM, LINE, COLOR.` · `JAAP SAID IT TOO.` · `LIGHT HAS NO COLOR, AND IS ALL COLOR.` · `NO OUTLINE, SO EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `NO FORM, NO COLOR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice what's behind the lids: maybe a dim glow, drifting specks, a soft darkness, no shapes worth naming. Don't try to make a picture; rest in the not-picture, and if an image of anything starts to form, let it fade. If you pray, you can hold the word Waheguru without picturing anything at all.
Rekh, a line, an outline. Roop na rekh na rang: no form, no outline, no color, and so able to be in every form and every color.
Your line: no form, no color. And so, the One can be in every color. See you tomorrow.

499.title: Beyond the three qualities
499.hook: He is beyond the three qualities that shape all things (Sukhmani 16)
499.tomorrow: Known by the one He blesses
499.howItsDone: Gurbani speaks of the three gunas and of a fourth state beyond them; Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's sixteenth salok hear that God is beyond all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rekh: no form, no outline, no color, and so able to be in every color. Today, the salok's next phrase: beyond the three qualities.

Monday morning, you're wired: fifteen tabs open, coffee half drunk, answering three people at once. Wednesday afternoon, you're heavy: you've read the same email four times and can't make yourself reply. And once in a while, a Saturday walk where everything is clear and quiet and kind. Three moods, sometimes in one week, sometimes in one hour. It's easy to treat them as simply who we are: personality, sleep, coffee. India's old philosophers gave those three a name, and the sixteenth ashtpadi uses it.

The salok says God is trihu gun te bhinn: beyond the three gunas. Gun, or guna, means quality, or strand, like the strands twisted together to make a rope. In older Indian philosophy, everything in the world is woven from three such strands. Rajas: restless energy, drive, wanting, the Monday mood. Tamas: heaviness, dullness, inertia, the Wednesday afternoon. And sattva: clarity, calm, balance, the Saturday walk. Every person, every day, every meal and mood is some mix of the three. Gurbani takes this picture up. It speaks of maya, the world's pull, as made of three qualities, and it's honest about all three, even the nice one. You might expect calm sattva to be the goal. But the One is beyond all three, the calm included. The three are weather. Good weather is lovely, but it still comes and goes. So Gurbani speaks of a fourth state, chautha pad, where a person rests in the One rather than in whatever mood is passing through. That's surprisingly practical. If calm were the goal, every restless morning would be a failure. If the goal is beyond all three, wired, heavy and clear are just strands passing by. You can notice them without being them. You can have a terrible Wednesday afternoon and still stand on something that isn't Wednesday afternoon. The salok is describing God. It's also describing a place to stand.
screen: `GUNA: A STRAND OF THE ROPE.` · `RESTLESS, HEAVY, CLEAR.` · `EVEN CALM IS WEATHER.` · `CHAUTHA PAD: THE FOURTH STATE.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE MOODS.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, without judging: is something restless in me right now, something heavy, something clear? Notice each one, without grabbing even the clear one. Let all three pass like weather, and rest in whatever is noticing them; if you pray, rest in Waheguru.
Trai gun, the three qualities. The One is beyond restless rajas, heavy tamas, and even calm sattva, and beyond all three.
Your line: beyond the moods. Even calm is weather, and the One is beyond all three. That's day four hundred ninety-nine.

500.title: Known by the one He blesses
500.hook: He is known by whom He chooses to be known (Sukhmani 16)
500.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of nadar, God's grace, as what finally opens the way, while keeping up daily effort in nitnem, seva and simran; the sixteenth salok of Sukhmani Sahib ends on this note.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trai gun: restless, heavy and even calm are weather, and the One is beyond all three. Today, the salok's last phrase, on a fitting day.

Five hundred days. If you've come this far, you've opened this path five hundred times, more than a year's worth of days. You might be tempted to think you've earned something: a level, a closeness, an understanding. And in a way you have. You know words and stories you didn't know. But the sixteenth ashtpadi ends its salok with a line that gently turns the milestone around. Knowing God, it says, isn't something you collect, like miles on a running app.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `HAVE YOU EARNED SOMETHING?` → `NOT MILES ON A RUNNING APP.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of the salok, in paraphrase: Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Bujhaae: He causes to understand. Suprasann: well pleased, delighted. So understanding God isn't seized. It's given, by the One, to whomever the One delights in. The Sikh word for that giving is nadar: grace, the glance of favor, literally a look. Japji Sahib puts it in a famous pair: by karma, by your actions, you receive this body like a garment; by nadar, by grace, you find the gate of liberation. Both halves matter. Actions are real and shape your life. But the final door opens from the other side. That can sound unfair, as if effort doesn't count. Sikhs don't read it that way. Look at how the tradition lives: rising early, reciting the banis, serving in the langar, remembering the Name all day. That's a lot of effort. But the effort isn't a payment that buys grace. It's more like opening the curtains. You can't make the sun rise. You can open the curtains every morning, so that when the light comes, it gets in. That's how many Sikhs describe their own daily discipline. The salok's grace is not a wage but a glance, given where the One is pleased. The posture it points to is waiting with the curtains open: not grabbing, and not keeping score.

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up and open, and don't reach for any special feeling. Be like a room with the curtains open in the early morning, ready for whatever light comes and fine if it's still gray. Each time you notice yourself straining, open your hands a little more; if you pray, let Waheguru be the only word, and let even that be quiet.
Nadar, grace, the glance of favor. The One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in. Effort opens the curtains; nadar is the light.
Your line: known by grace. You can't make the sun rise, but the curtains are yours to open. Day five hundred, with thanks.

501.title: Living ashtpadi 16
501.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 17, salok: true in the beginning
501.howItsDone: Sikhs commonly call God Nirankaar, the Formless, and Gurbani describes the One as both nirgun and sargun, without and with qualities, pervading everything; gurdwaras keep no image of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar: grace, a glance that's given, not a wage that's earned. Today we close the sixteenth ashtpadi by living it, in the simplest place there is.

An apartment, the day before you move in. Not a cluttered room; a properly empty one. Bare floor, bare walls, a window. What's in it? Nothing, you'd say. But that's not quite right. The room is full of space. You can't see it, paint it or pick it up, and yet it's what makes the room any use. You'll put a bed in it, a table, a life, and every one of those things will sit inside that invisible, shapeless room-ness.
screen: `AN EMPTY ROOM.` → `WHAT'S IN IT? NOTHING.` → `ACTUALLY, FULL OF SPACE.`

segments.voice: This week's salok said God has no form, no outline, no color, is beyond the three qualities, and is known by grace. Gurbani takes one more step. The One is nirankaar, formless: nir, without; aakaar, shape. Sikhs use it as a name for God: Nirankaar. But Guru Arjan, elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, pairs the two in one breath: formless, and Himself every form; without qualities, and with qualities, one. Nirgun and sargun. Both, at once. It sounds like a riddle. The empty room makes it less of one. Space has no shape, and that's exactly why it can hold every shape. If space were square, round things wouldn't fit. Because it's nothing in particular, it can be around everything in particular. Sikh teaching also says the One is sarab viaapak, pervading all: not sitting at the top of the sky, but in and through every thing, the way space is in and through every room. That's why the formlessness isn't cold. Anything with a shape is over there, in one place and not another. The Formless has no edge to stop at. So the One is also right here: in the kitchen, on the bus, in the hospital waiting room. For someone living the sixteenth ashtpadi, the quiet corner, the bare wall, the space between the furniture aren't nothing. They make a fair picture of what has no picture.

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on a blank stretch of wall or floor, or on the air in the middle of the room, and look at the space between things rather than the things. Notice that it's everywhere: around you, inside your cupped hands, between your breaths. If you pray, let Waheguru be the name of that everywhere.
Nirankaar, the Formless. No shape of its own, and so able to be in and through every shape, like space in an empty room.
Your line: formless, everywhere. No edge to stop at, so the One is right here too. See you tomorrow.

502.title: Ashtpadi 17, salok: true in the beginning
502.hook: aad sach: the same salok as Japji's opening returns (Sukhmani 17)
502.howItsDone: Sikhs recite aad sach, jugaad sach as the salok after the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and meet the same salok again at the opening of Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirankaar: formless, and so everywhere, like space in an empty room. Today the seventeenth ashtpadi opens with words you've heard before.

You're halfway through a long, new song, and suddenly the band plays the opening bars of one you've known since childhood. It stops you. You know where you are. Something like that happens at the seventeenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani. After sixteen ashtpadis of Guru Arjan's own words, the salok is a line Sikhs know from the very first page of the Guru Granth Sahib: the line right after the Mool Mantar, which opens Japji Sahib every morning. Words Sikhs know as Guru Nanak's, coming back inside Guru Arjan's hymn.
screen: `A NEW SONG, THEN AN OLD ONE.` → `THE FIRST PAGE OF THE GURU.` → `GURU NANAK'S WORDS RETURN.`

segments.voice: Here it is in Punjabi first, the way it's recited every morning. Aad sach, jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach, Nanak, hosee bhee sach. In paraphrase: true in the beginning, true through the ages. True now, Nanak, and true it will be. Sach is truth, and in Gurbani it means more than not lying. Sach is what's real, what lasts, what holds. The line walks it through every kind of time. Aad: the beginning, before anything began. Jugaad: through the ages, the long eras of the world. Hai bhee: is, right now. Hosee bhee: will be, after everything we know is gone. Four steps, and the truth is the same at every one. Why would Guru Arjan bring it back here? Sukhmani doesn't say, and the sources don't record his reason, so we can only notice what it does. It ties the hymn to the root of the scripture: Sukhmani by the fifth Guru, Japji by the first. Sikhs hear in it one teaching passed from Guru to Guru, like one flame lit from another; they describe the Gurus that way, ten bodies, one light. It also helps anyone reciting Sukhmani, a long recitation. Deep in the middle, when attention fades, here is a line the tongue already knows. You come home to it. And it sets up what follows: the seventeenth ashtpadi is about truth, and it starts by saying truth doesn't change with the times.

segments.voice: Say it once, slowly: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach, or in English, true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, true to come. Then let it settle, and bring to mind one thing in your life that was true at the start and is still true now. Rest there.
Sach, truth, what's real and lasts. The salok is Japji's: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach, true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and to come.
Your line: true then, true now. Moods and news shift, and the line doesn't. Day five hundred two, done.

503.title: True is His court
503.hook: true is the Lord, true His court, true His works (Sukhmani 17)
503.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi repeat sat, true, through line after line, and Gurbani speaks of the sachee dargah, God's true court, where each life is seen as it really was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, true to come. Today the stanzas run that truth through everything.

The cashier is busy and distracted, and she hands you change for a fifty when you gave her a twenty. Nobody saw. The store is a big chain; it won't miss thirty dollars. You're halfway to the door. It's a small pause: the moment where the truth costs something and nobody would ever know. The seventeenth ashtpadi has an answer for that pause, and it isn't a rule. It's a description of what the world is made of.
screen: `CHANGE FOR A FIFTY, NOT A TWENTY.` → `NOBODY SAW.` → `HALFWAY TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of the seventeenth ashtpadi is built almost entirely out of one word, repeated: sat. True. In paraphrase: true are His feet, and true the one who touches them. True His worship, true the one who serves. True His sight, true the one who sees. True His Name, true the one who remembers it. True the Word, and true the One who speaks it. Line after line, sat, sat, sat, until truth isn't a single fact anymore but the material everything is made of. Today's title adds an image from elsewhere in Gurbani: the dargah. Dargah is a Persian word for a royal court, where a ruler sits and cases are heard. In Gurbani, the dargah is God's court, where every life is finally seen as it really was, and Gurbani calls it the sachee dargah, the true court. Not a court where the clever win, or the rich, or the well-connected. A court where only what's real counts. Put those together and truth isn't one rule among many. It's the grain of the wood. A lie isn't just breaking a rule; it cuts against the grain of everything. Read that way, the cashier moment changes. The question stops being, will anyone know? In the ashtpadi's picture of a world that's true all through, the thirty dollars is already known, not by a camera, but by the way things are. Handing it back isn't heroic. It's going with the grain.

Your line: true all through. Truth is the grain of the wood, not one rule among many. Until tomorrow.

504.title: True are His devotees
504.hook: those who live in truth become true (Sukhmani 17)
504.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi hear each true thing paired with the person who meets it, and Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, the stone that turns iron to gold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dargah: the true court, and a world where truth is the grain of everything. Today, what truth does to people.

Spend a summer with someone who has a strong accent and you'll come home with a little of it. Live with a person who's always on time and you start, grudgingly, to be on time. We take on the shape of what we're near. Parents notice it with their kids' friends; managers notice it with teams. Gurbani has an old picture for this, about a stone and a piece of iron. And the seventeenth ashtpadi has a line that points the same way.
screen: `A SUMMER, AND YOU COME HOME WITH AN ACCENT.` → `WE TAKE THE SHAPE OF WHAT WE'RE NEAR.` → `A STONE AND A PIECE OF IRON.`

segments.voice: Look at yesterday's stanza again. Every line had two halves. True are His feet, and true the one who touches them. True His worship, and true the one who serves. True the Name, and true the one who remembers it. The second half is always a person. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: for the one who understands, everything becomes true. So the truth doesn't stay with God. It spreads to whoever comes near it. The devotee, the bhagat, isn't true by birth, or by being clever about truth. They become true by touching what's true, again and again. Gurbani's picture for this is the paras, the philosopher's stone of Indian legend, which turns iron into gold just by touching it. Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, and Sikhs say the same of the sangat, the company of the good. You don't become gold by thinking about gold. You become gold by contact. That makes truth practical. It isn't mainly an argument you win; it's a substance you're near, or not. In Sikh life, one way people stay near it is small, repeated faithfulness: the morning banis, said every day; the word kept; the promise honored when it's inconvenient. Every kept promise is a little contact with the true. In this picture, nobody becomes true in one heroic act. It happens the way iron becomes gold in the old story: touch by touch.
screen: `TRUE THING, TRUE PERSON: EACH LINE.` · `BHAGAT: THE DEVOTEE.` · `PARAS: IRON TURNED TO GOLD.` · `A KEPT PROMISE IS CONTACT.` · then, large: `BECOME TRUE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the week for one small promise you made and haven't kept yet: a call, a returned book, a 'let's get coffee' you didn't mean. Picture yourself keeping it, simply, without announcing it, as a kind of touch, contact with what's true. If you pray, say Waheguru as you decide.
Paras, the legendary stone that turns iron to gold. The bhagat becomes true by touching the true, like iron turned to gold: touch by touch.
Your line: become true. Iron doesn't turn to gold by thinking about gold. Rest well.
